walkthroughs.title: R: the unit of risk
steps: Before you buy, find the price that proves you wrong. Entry minus that stop is R, your initial risk.
Count every result in R. Risk $10 and make $100, and that's a 10R winner.
Average your R over a lot of trades and you've got your expectancy: what one trade is worth to you.

walkthroughs.title: Drawdown and ruin
steps: A drawdown is the drop from your account's high to the low after it, as a percent.
Losses are harder to fix than they look. Lose 50% and you need 100% just to get back.
Risk too much per trade and a normal losing streak can finish you. That's risk of ruin.
So we keep it small. Under 1% a trade is normal, and 2% is the absolute ceiling.

walkthroughs.title: Stops that follow the trend
steps: Your first stop sets R. As the trade works, the stop moves up. Never down, never wider.
A trailing stop follows price. The Chandelier Exit hangs it three ATRs under the 22-day high.
We keep it simpler: the 9 EMA for fast movers, the 20 EMA for steadier ones.
Too tight and normal wiggles knock you out. Too loose and a real reversal eats your profit.

questions.q: Your plan reads: buy at $50, stop at $48.50. Before you size it, you need your R. What is R?
choices: Your planned loss, entry to stop
The money you put into the trade
The gain you expect at your target
questions.answer: Your planned loss, entry to stop
questions.why: Your planned loss, entry to stop. Here that's $50 down to $48.50. It's what being wrong costs you on each share, and you know it before you click buy. Everything else runs off it. The share count comes from it, and every result gets counted in it. Get R wrong and the size is wrong too.
questions.lesson_line: Know what being wrong costs before you buy. That's your R.

wrong.The money you put into the trade: That's your position size. You risk far less than you put in, because the stop gets you out first.
wrong.The stock's average daily range: That's ATR, how far the stock moves in a normal day. It helps you place a stop, but it isn't your risk.
wrong.The gain you expect at your target: That's the reward side. R is the risk side, entry down to the stop.

questions.simple: R is the loss you plan for, the gap from your entry down to your stop.

deeper.example: Van Tharp calls it the initial risk, R for short: the difference between your stop and your entry. He's clear that the amount risked is not the amount invested.

questions.q: You buy a breakout at $100 and set your stop at $96, under the low of the day. What's your R per share?
questions.why: $4 a share. $100 minus $96 is $4, and that's 1R. It's 4% of your price, inside the 5% we'll accept on a stop. Every number after this runs off that $4: the share count, your targets, how you grade the result. Write it down before you buy.
questions.lesson_line: Entry minus stop. That's 1R per share.
questions.simple: Your R is $4 a share, the gap from your $100 buy down to your $96 stop.

wrong.$0.40: A slipped decimal. $100 minus $96 is $4, not 40 cents.
wrong.$96: That's the stop price. R is the distance down to it.
wrong.$104: You added the $4 to your entry. The stop sits under your buy, so you subtract.

deeper.example: Tharp's own example buys at $50 and sells if it drops to $40, so 1R is $10 a share.

questions.q: You buy $4,000 of stock with a stop that would cost you $1,000. Your R on this trade is the $4,000.
questions.why: False. The $4,000 is what you put in. R is what you lose if the stop hits, and here that's $1,000. Mix those two up and you'll size every trade wrong. You'd only lose the whole $4,000 if the stock went to zero, and your stop gets you out long before that. R can mean the risk per share or on the whole position.
questions.lesson_line: Invested and risked are two different numbers. R is the risked one.
questions.simple: False. R is what you lose at your stop, not the money you put into the stock.

reasons: fixed before (checker added a second publisher)

deeper.example: This is Tharp's own example: you buy $4,000 worth of stock but risk only $1,000, 1% of the account. He warns the amount risked should not be confused with the amount invested.

questions.story: You buy 200 shares at $30. Your stop sits at $28.50, a few cents under the low of the day.
questions.q: If the stop hits, how much do you lose?
questions.why: $300. $30 minus $28.50 is $1.50 a share. Times 200 shares, that's $300. That's the number your account feels if you're wrong, so it's the number you size from. The $6,000 is what the shares cost. You'd only lose all of it if the stock went to zero.
questions.lesson_line: Risk per share times shares. That's the number your account feels.

wrong.$1.50: That's the loss on one share. You hold 200 of them.
wrong.$6,000: That's what the position cost. Your stop gets you out long before the stock goes to zero.
wrong.$5,700: That's what your shares are worth at the stop, not what you lose.

questions.simple: You lose $300, $1.50 a share on all 200 shares, if the stop hits.

questions.q: The risk on your trade is how much the stock bounces around in a day.
questions.why: False. Your risk is a distance you pick: from your entry down to your stop, the most you're willing to lose. How much a stock bounces is its volatility. That still matters, because a stop inside the normal bounce gets hit for no reason. So a jumpy stock gets a stop outside its noise, and you buy fewer shares.
questions.lesson_line: Your risk is a distance you choose. The stock's swing is why you choose it with care.
questions.simple: False. Your risk is the gap from your entry to your stop, the most you'll lose, not how much price swings.

deeper.trap: Van Tharp makes the point himself: his risk is the distance from entry to the worst loss you're willing to take, much different from the academic idea of risk as variability. A finance class means price swings. A trade plan means what you lose at the stop.

questions.q: Your trade journal has a column for each trade's R-multiple. What goes in it?
choices: A trade's result counted in R
questions.answer: A trade's result counted in R
questions.why: The trade's result counted in R. Take the profit or loss and divide it by the risk you planned, entry to stop. Make 10 times your risk and that's a 10R winner. Lose exactly what you planned and it's 1R lost. Counting this way puts a cheap stock and an expensive one on the same scale.
questions.lesson_line: Count every result in R and every trade speaks the same language.

wrong.Your stop distance in ATRs: That's how you'd measure an ATR stop. An R-multiple measures the result.
wrong.Winning trades divided by losers: That counts trades. It says nothing about how big each win or loss was.
wrong.Your share count times R: That's your total risk on the position, not the result.

questions.simple: It's the trade's result counted in R, the profit or loss divided by the risk you planned.

deeper.example: Tharp's glossary: a 10R multiple is a profit 10 times the initial risk. Risk $10 and make $100, and that's a 10R-multiple profit.

questions.q: You bought at $80 with a stop at $76. You sold into a strong push at $92. What did the trade make in R?
questions.why: 3R. Your risk was $80 minus $76, $4 a share. Your gain was $92 minus $80, $12 a share. $12 over $4 is 3R. Log it that way. Then every trade in your journal speaks the same language, whatever the stock costs.
questions.lesson_line: Divide what you made by what you risked. That's the R-multiple.
questions.simple: You made 3R, because your $12 gain is three times the $4 you risked.

wrong.12R: That's the $12 gain per share. You still have to divide by the $4 risk.
wrong.4R: That's the $4 risk per share, not the multiple.
wrong.0.33R: Upside down. That's the risk divided by the gain.

deeper.example: Tharp's drill works the same way: buy at $40, plan to exit at $35, sell at $50. That's $10 on $5 of risk, a 2R profit.

questions.q: If the stock gaps down through your stop, the loss can be bigger than 1R.
questions.why: True. The stop turns into a market order, and the fill can be far from the stop price. Tharp: losses bigger than 1R happen all the time.
questions.lesson_line: 1R is the plan, not a promise. Aim to keep every loss at 1R or less.

questions.story: You buy at $100 with a stop at $97, a 3% risk. It trades down to $97 and you don't sell. You're hoping. You finally get out at $91.
questions.q: What did that trade cost you in R?
questions.why: -3R. You planned to lose $3 a share, $100 down to $97. You sold at $91, $9 under your buy. $9 over $3 is 3R lost. The stop was the plan, and hoping tripled the loss. I almost never take a loss greater than 3%. That only works because I sell when the stop hits, not when it feels better.
questions.lesson_line: The stop is the plan. Skip it and the loss multiplies.

wrong.-1R: That's the loss you planned at $97. You held past it.
wrong.-0.33R: Upside down. That's your risk divided by your loss.
wrong.-9R: That's the $9 drop per share. Divide it by the $3 you risked.

questions.simple: It's a -3R loss. You planned to lose $3 a share and lost $9 by holding past the stop.

deeper.trap: Hoping is how a 1R loss grows. Tharp's own drill skips a $55 stop on a $60 buy and ends with a 12R loss. That's why every stop sits with the broker as a real order, not in your head.

questions.q: You sold some of a winner into a 5-day push. The stock is still trending. What do you do with the rest?
choices: Trail it under the 9 or 20 EMA
Sell the rest right now too
Hold it to a set percent gain
Sell it at a 2R profit target
questions.answer: Trail it under the 9 or 20 EMA
questions.why: Trail it. You've already paid yourself into the push, so the rest gets room to run. Fast movers ride the 9 EMA, steadier ones the 20 EMA. Sell what's left on a close below that line. The first sell was a judgment too. We rarely sell on day 1, and selling into a 3, 5 or 7 day push is often best.
questions.lesson_line: Sell some into the push. Trail the rest and let the line take you out.

wrong.Sell the rest right now too: That ends the trade on a stock that's still trending. The trail keeps you in for the next leg.
wrong.Hold it to a set percent gain: A fixed percent ignores how the stock is acting. The trail follows the trend instead.
wrong.Sell it at a 2R profit target: We don't sell the last part at a fixed 2R. It trails until the line breaks.

questions.simple: Trail the rest under the 9 or 20 EMA and sell it on a close below the line.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B19, E51, E52)

questions.q: Your journal says your expectancy is positive. What is that number telling you?
choices: The share of trades that win
What you hope this trade makes
questions.why: Your average result per trade. Add up every win and loss in R and divide by the number of trades. It weighs how often you win and how big the wins and losses are, both at once. Positive means the way you trade makes money over many trades. That's the number I'd check before I ever sized up.
questions.lesson_line: Expectancy is what one trade is worth, on average, over many trades.

wrong.The share of trades that win: That's your win rate. It leaves out how big the wins and losses are.
wrong.Your biggest win so far: One trade says nothing about the average.
wrong.What you hope this trade makes: That's a target. Expectancy is an average over many trades.

questions.simple: It's your average result per trade, what all your wins and losses work out to.

deeper.example: Tharp calls expectancy the mean R-multiple, best stated per dollar you risk. Schwab says to track your trading history to find your average gain or loss per trade.

questions.q: Your log: you win 40% of your trades. Winners average 3R, losers 1R. What's your expectancy per trade?
questions.why: 0.6R a trade. Weight each result by how often it happens. Wins: 40% of the time at 3R is 1.2R. Losses: the rest of the time at 1R is 0.6R. 1.2R minus 0.6R leaves 0.6R. You lose more often than you win and still make money, because the winners are three times the losers.
questions.lesson_line: Expectancy needs both: how often you win, and how big the wins and losses are.
questions.simple: Your expectancy is 0.6R a trade, because your 3R wins more than pay for your 1R losses.

wrong.1.2R: That counts the wins and forgets the losses.
wrong.2R: That's the 3R win minus the 1R loss. It ignores how often each one happens.
wrong.1.4R: You swapped the rates, as if the winners came 60% of the time.

deeper.example: Tharp calls expectancy the mean R-multiple. Investopedia's expected value is the same sum: each outcome times how likely it is, added up.

questions.q: Your method has a positive expectancy, so the next trade you take will make money.
questions.why: False. Expectancy is an average over many trades. It says nothing about the next one. A good method still loses trades, sometimes several in a row. That's why you size small enough to sit through the losing runs. Judge your method on the whole sample, never on the last trade.
questions.lesson_line: An edge shows up over many trades, not on the next one.
questions.simple: False. Expectancy is an average over many trades, so any single trade can still lose.

deeper.trap: The trap is judging your method by its last trade. One loss doesn't prove the edge is gone, and one win doesn't prove it works. Tharp sizes a trade so it survives the worst short-term run and still collects the long-term average.

questions.story: Your new setup has 8 closed trades. They average +1.5R.
questions.q: What does that tell you about its expectancy?
choices: Too few trades to trust yet
It's proven, so size up now
questions.answer: Too few trades to trust yet
questions.why: Too few trades to trust yet. Tharp wants at least thirty trades for a good idea of expectancy, and 100 to 200 for a clear picture.
questions.lesson_line: Eight trades is a story, not a statistic. Keep logging them.

wrong.It earns 1.5R a trade: That's what 8 trades did. A small sample can sit far from the true average.
wrong.It's proven, so size up now: Tharp says start small and size up only after months of proof, not days.

questions.q: Tap the word that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: Average the R-multiples of all your trades and you get your ___.
questions.why: Expectancy. Tharp: expectancy is simply the mean, or average, R-multiple a system generates. Schwab calls it your average gain or loss per trade. Win rate only counts how often you win.
questions.lesson_line: Log every trade in R. The average is your expectancy.
questions.simple: Expectancy, because the average of your R-multiples is what one trade earns you on average.

reasons: fixed before (checker added a second publisher)

questions.story: Plan A wins 30% of the time, with +4R winners and -1R losers. Plan B wins 70%, with +0.5R winners and -2R losers.
questions.q: Which plan would you rather trade?
questions.why: Plan A, at +0.5R a trade. A wins 30% of the time at +4R, which is +1.2R. It loses the rest of the time at -1R, and that nets +0.5R. B feels better because it wins 70% of the time. But each 2R loss wipes out four 0.5R wins, and B ends up below zero. I'd take the plan that pays, not the one that feels good.
questions.lesson_line: Always weigh how often you win by how much you win or lose.

wrong.B, at +0.35R a trade: That counts B's wins and forgets its losses.
wrong.B, because it wins more: Winning often isn't enough when each loss is four times a win.
wrong.A, at +1.2R a trade: That's A's winners alone. Take off the losers.

questions.simple: Plan A. Its big wins pay for its losses, while each of B's 2R losses eats four of its small wins.

deeper.trap: Plan B is easier to live with, because it wins 70% of the time. But it loses the other 30%, and each 2R loss costs four 0.5R wins. Tharp notes that some systems with a high hit rate still lose money through occasional large losses.

questions.q: You closed 20 trades this month and 9 of them made money. Which number does that give you?
questions.why: Win rate. It's how often your closed trades made money, here 9 out of 20. It says nothing about how much. A low win rate can make money with big winners, and a high one can lose with big losers. So I never read it alone. Look at it next to your average win and loss in R.
questions.lesson_line: Win rate counts how often you win. It never says how much.

wrong.Expectancy: That's your average result per trade. It weighs the size of the wins and losses too.
wrong.R-multiple: That's one trade's result counted in R.
wrong.Risk/reward ratio: That's one trade's plan, stop against target, not your record.

questions.simple: Win rate. It counts how often your closed trades made money, not how much.

deeper.example: Tharp defines win rate as the percentage of closed trades in which you make money. Investopedia agrees: winning trades out of all trades.

questions.story: Over 100 trades, 99 lose $1 each. One trade makes $500.
questions.q: Your win rate is 1%. What's the net result?
questions.why: A $401 profit. The 99 losers cost $1 each, $99 in all. The one winner made $500, and $500 minus $99 is $401. You lost 99 times out of 100 and still made money. That's why win rate alone tells you nothing. The size of the winners decides it.
questions.lesson_line: A low win rate can pay and a high one can lose. Check the sizes.

wrong.A $99 loss: That counts the losers and forgets the one big winner.
wrong.A $4.01 gain: That's the average per trade, the $401 spread over 100 trades. The question asks for the net.

questions.simple: You net a $401 profit, because the one $500 winner is bigger than the 99 losses of $1.

deeper.counter: This is Tharp's own example. It works the other way too. Investopedia: if the losses are three times as large as the gains, more wins than losses is still a losing strategy.

reasons: one publisher only (Van Tharp Institute) for the key

questions.q: You're planning a buy with a stop and a target. What does the trade's risk/reward compare?
choices: Loss at the stop vs gain at the target
Your winning trades vs your losers
Your risk vs your account size
Today's range vs the average range
questions.answer: Loss at the stop vs gain at the target
questions.why: Loss at the stop against gain at the target, both measured from your entry. Ask it before every buy: is the reward worth the risk. It describes one trade's plan, not your record. And it's only as good as the stop. A stop placed to make the ratio look good isn't a real stop.
questions.lesson_line: Before you buy, know both distances: to the stop and to the target.

wrong.Your winning trades vs your losers: That's a count of wins and losses, not one trade's plan.
wrong.Your risk vs your account size: That's your risk per trade as a share of the account. Risk/reward compares two distances on one trade.
wrong.Today's range vs the average range: That's a read on how jumpy the stock is today.

questions.simple: It compares what you lose if the stop hits with what you make if the target hits.

deeper.example: Investopedia measures entry to the stop against entry to the take-profit order. Tharp says to ask before every trade whether the potential reward is worth the potential risk.

questions.q: Entry $20, stop $19, and your target is the old high at $23. How many dollars can you make for each dollar you risk?
questions.why: $3. The target is $23 minus $20, $3 away. The stop is $20 minus $19, $1 away. $3 over $1 is $3 for every $1 you risk, which people write as 1:3. Just don't let the ratio pick your stop. The chart picks the stop, then you check if the reward is worth it.
questions.lesson_line: Divide the distance to the target by the distance to the stop.
questions.simple: You make $3 for each $1 you risk, because the target is three times as far as the stop.

wrong.$4: You measured the reward from the stop, not from your entry.
wrong.$0.33: Upside down. That's the risk divided by the reward.
wrong.$1.15: You divided the target price by the entry price.

questions.story: You buy at $50. The low of the day is $48.50 and your stop sits just under it. Your target is $56. To make the ratio look better, you pull the stop up to $49.60.
questions.q: What did that tighter stop cost you?
choices: More chance the stop is hit
questions.answer: More chance the stop is hit
questions.why: More chance the stop is hit. Your loss per share shrank, and the ratio looks great on paper. But $49.60 sits inside today's range, where the normal wiggles live. The stock can dip there and come right back. So you swapped a real stop for a coin flip. The stop goes where the chart says you're wrong, and the size comes from it.
questions.lesson_line: Never move the stop to make the ratio pretty. The chart sets the stop.

wrong.Nothing, the trade got safer: The loss per share shrank, but the odds of getting shaken out went way up.
wrong.Your protection from a gap: No stop protects you from a gap, at $48.50 or at $49.60.
wrong.Some of your upside to $56: The target didn't move. Only the stop did.

questions.simple: It raised the chance the stop is hit, because $49.60 sits inside the normal swings.

deeper.trap: Judging a trade by its ratio alone is the trap. Investopedia makes the point: a tighter stop shrinks the loss, but it raises the odds the price action triggers it. Stop first, then the size.

questions.q: Your stop is marked a few cents under the low of the day. What does position sizing decide from here?
questions.why: How many shares to buy. You've already picked the stock and the stop. Sizing takes the dollars you're willing to lose and divides them by your risk per share. That gives you the share count. It never moves the stop. If the honest stop doesn't fit your risk, you skip the trade.
questions.lesson_line: The stop comes first. Sizing turns it into a share count.

wrong.Where to put your stop: The chart picks the stop. Sizing uses its distance.
wrong.Which stock to buy: That's your setup and your watchlist.

questions.simple: It decides how many shares to buy, from your stop and what you're willing to lose.

deeper.example: Investopedia: sizing decides how many units to buy, given the account size and risk tolerance. Tharp calls it the part of your system that controls how much you trade.

questions.q: Account $40,000, risking 1% a trade. Entry $50, stop $48.50 under the low of the day. How many shares do you buy?
questions.why: 266 shares. 1% of $40,000 is $400 at risk. $50 minus $48.50 is $1.50 a share. $400 over $1.50 is 266.67, and you round down to 266. Always down: rounding up risks more than you planned. The stop sits 3% under your buy, a good spot. The position also stays under our 40% cap, so the risk sets the size.
questions.lesson_line: Dollars at risk over risk per share. Round down, never up.
questions.simple: Buy 266 shares. $400 of risk over $1.50 a share is 266.67, rounded down.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A5, A7)

wrong.400 shares: That's the $400 of risk read as a share count.
wrong.800 shares: That spends the whole $40,000 at $50 and ignores the stop.

deeper.example: Investopedia's method is the same: divide the account risk by the trade risk. Their $500 over $20 gives 25 shares.

questions.q: Everyone talks about the 2% rule. What does it actually cap?
choices: Your risk per trade to 2% of capital
Each position to 2% of the account
Your stop to 2% under your entry price
Your losses in any one month to 2%
questions.answer: Your risk per trade to 2% of capital
questions.why: Your risk per trade, at 2% of the account. It caps what you lose if the stop hits, not how much you buy. Risk 2% with a tight stop and the position can be far bigger than 2%. For us 2% is the absolute ceiling, and under 1% is normal. A gap can still push a real loss past it, so size for that too.
questions.lesson_line: The 2% rule caps risk, not position size.

wrong.Each position to 2% of the account: That mixes up risk and size. A 2% risk can sit on a much bigger position.
wrong.Your stop to 2% under your entry price: The chart sets the stop. The rule caps the dollars you lose there.
wrong.Your losses in any one month to 2%: That's a different rule. Our monthly brake is 8%: hit it and you're done for the month.

questions.simple: It caps what you lose on one trade, at the stop, at 2% of your account.

deeper.counter: A 2% risk doesn't mean a 2% position. In Tharp's magazine example you buy $10,000 of stock, yet your initial risk is only $1,000. The stop distance sets how big the position can be.

reasons: the why names the owner's rulebook A1 ceiling (2%)
fixed before (key changed from loss to risk)

questions.q: You hold a stock overnight with a stop under it. Bad news hits after the close. What's gap risk?
choices: Your stop sits too far away
questions.why: Price opens right past your stop. The stop still triggers, but it sells at the next price there is, not at your stop price. So the loss can be well beyond what you planned, and good sizing can't stop that. It's why a tight stop never earns a monster position. It's also why we don't buy in the 3 days before earnings.
questions.lesson_line: A stop picks when you sell, not the price you get in a gap.

wrong.Your stop sits too far away: That's a stop you placed badly. Gap risk is price jumping past the stop.
wrong.The stock drifts sideways: That costs you time, not a gap.
wrong.Your order fills in parts: That's a partial fill, an order issue.

questions.simple: Price jumps past your stop at the open, so you sell lower than planned and lose more.

deeper.example: Investopedia: even proper position sizing can't stop you losing more than you meant to if a stock gaps beyond your stop. Schwab: after a gap down, the fill can be far below the stop price.

questions.story: You risk 1% of the account. Entry $50, with a real stop order at $48.50 sitting with your broker. Bad news hits overnight and the stock opens at $47.
questions.q: Roughly how much of the account did you lose?
choices: Nothing yet, the gap skipped it
About 6%, as far as it fell
questions.why: About 2%, double what you planned. Your stop turned into a market order at the open and sold near $47. You planned to lose $1.50 a share, $50 down to $48.50. The gap cost you $3, $50 down to $47. Twice the distance means twice the loss, about 2% instead of 1%. That's the cost of holding overnight.
questions.lesson_line: Plan your size for the gap, not just for the stop.

wrong.1%, your stop capped the loss: A stop can't fill at a price the stock never traded. It sold near the $47 open.
wrong.Nothing yet, the gap skipped it: A gap through the stop still triggers it. It sells at the next price there is.
wrong.About 6%, as far as it fell: That's how far the stock fell. Your account lost what your size made it lose, about twice the 1% you planned.

questions.simple: About 2%. The stop sold at the $47 open, twice as far down as you planned.

deeper.trap: A stop is a trigger, not a floor. Investopedia warns that slippage and gap risk can make a loss significantly greater than planned. That's why a tight stop never justifies a bigger position: a gap can jump the stop.

reasons: touches the owner's gap rule (B20), flagged

questions.story: You hold a stock into its earnings report tomorrow. The trade is up 2R. Your stop is $2 under the price, and a $4 gap down is possible.
questions.q: Under UCT's rule, what do you do before the report?
choices: Sell it all before the report
Halve the size and hold the rest
Hold, the stop caps the loss
questions.answer: Sell it all before the report
questions.why: Sell it all before the report. Our rule: hold through a report only if the trade is up 5R. Up 2R, you are out before it. No stop protects you in a gap. A gap through the stop fills at the next available price. A $4 gap is twice your $2 stop. Halving the size, Investopedia's idea, still leaves half the position exposed.
questions.lesson_line: A stop can't stop a gap. We hold through earnings only when up 5R.

wrong.Switch to a stop-limit order: In a gap it may not fill at all, and you'd still hold the stock into the report.
wrong.Halve the size and hold the rest: That's Investopedia's way to cut gap risk. Our rule is stricter: under 5R, nothing is held through a report.
wrong.Hold, the stop caps the loss: A gap fills at the next available price, past the stop. We hold only trades up 5R.

questions.simple: Sell before the report, because our rule holds through earnings only when a trade is up 5R, and this one is up 2R.

deeper.trap: The trap is trusting the stop. A stop sets when you sell, not the price you get. If the stock opens $4 lower, the stop triggers and fills near the open, about twice the loss you planned. That is why our rule clears trades under 5R out before the report instead of hoping the stop holds.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook B22 (hold through a report only if up 5R)
a rule the owner has already changed once (the day count)

questions.q: Before you buy, you mark a stop a few cents under the low of the day. What job is that stop doing?
choices: Sets where you get out if wrong
Locks in the exact price you sell at
Picks where you will take your profit
Sets how many shares you should buy
questions.answer: Sets where you get out if wrong
questions.why: It sets where you get out if you're wrong. You pick that spot before you buy, while you're calm. The stop price is a trigger. Once it hits, the order sells at market, so the fill can come in a bit lower. It doesn't pick your target. Your share count comes after, from its distance.
questions.lesson_line: Decide where you're wrong before you buy. That's the stop.

wrong.Locks in the exact price you sell at: It sets an exit, not a price. Once hit it sells at market, and the fill can differ.
wrong.Picks where you will take your profit: That's the target, the reward side of the plan.
wrong.Sets how many shares you should buy: Sizing comes after the stop and uses its distance.

questions.simple: It marks where you get out if the trade is wrong, so you know your exit before you buy.

deeper.example: Tharp calls a stop a preplanned exit. The SEC says investors use sell stops to try to limit a loss on stock they own.

questions.q: It's fine to buy first and work out where your stop goes once you're in.
questions.why: False. The stop comes before the buy, every time. No stop, no size, no trade. We write the entry, the stop and the size down before the market opens. Once you're in and it's moving, you'll talk yourself into a stop that feels better, not one that's right. Decide while you're calm.
questions.lesson_line: No stop, no trade. The exit is part of the entry.
questions.simple: False. You set the stop before you open the trade, never after you're in.

reasons: the why teaches the owner's rulebook D39 (entry, stop and size written down before the open)

deeper.example: Tharp's golden rule: never open a position without knowing exactly where you'll exit. Schwab also says to specify how you'll close a trade before you place it.

questions.q: We set our stop a flat 8% under the price we pay.
questions.why: False. Our stop goes a few cents under the low of the day, or yesterday's low. That's where the chart says you're wrong. A flat 8% ignores the chart, and it's wider than we'll take. We like 1-3%, accept up to 5%, and past that we wait for a tighter trigger. The size then comes from the stop.
questions.lesson_line: A few cents under the low of the day. The chart sets the stop, not a percent.
questions.simple: False. Our stop goes a few cents under today's low or yesterday's low, not a flat percent.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A3, F62)

questions.q: Your account made a new high last month and has slid since. What does your drawdown measure?
choices: The drop from the peak to the low
Your loss below what you put in
Money you took out of the account
questions.answer: The drop from the peak to the low
questions.why: The drop from the peak to the low. You measure from the high, not from where you started. It counts open losses too, not just closed trades. So you can be in a drawdown and still be up overall. Watch it, because our size steps down as the drawdown grows.
questions.lesson_line: Drawdown is measured from the high, not from where you started.

wrong.The day's high-to-low range: That's one day's range, not a fall in your account.
wrong.Your loss below what you put in: A drawdown runs from the peak. You can be in one and still be in profit.
wrong.Money you took out of the account: That's a retirement drawdown, a withdrawal. In trading it means a fall in value.

questions.simple: It's the drop from the account's peak to its low, measured from the high, not from what you put in.

deeper.example: Investopedia's example: a stock bought at $100 rises to $110, then falls to $80. The drawdown is 27.3%, measured from the $110 peak. The trader's loss is only $20 a share, measured from the $100 they paid.

questions.story: You buy at $40. The stock runs to $60, then pulls back to $48.
questions.q: Where do you stand at $48?
choices: A 20% loss on the whole trade
No drawdown, since you're still up
questions.why: A 20% drawdown, and still a profit. Drawdown runs from the peak: $60 down to $48 is $12, and $12 over $60 is 20%. Profit runs from what you paid, and $48 is still above your $40. Both are true at once. That giveback is exactly what a trail is there to limit.
questions.lesson_line: A drawdown can happen inside a winner. It measures what you gave back.

wrong.A 20% loss on the whole trade: You paid $40. At $48 you're still up on the trade.
wrong.No drawdown, since you're still up: Drawdown is measured from the peak, not from your entry.
wrong.A 12% drawdown from the $60 peak: That's the $12 drop read as a percent. Divide it by the $60 peak.

questions.simple: A 20% drawdown but still a profit. Drawdown runs from the $60 peak, profit from your $40 buy.

reasons: choices rebalanced (the key was the longest)

deeper.example: Investopedia makes the same point: a drawdown isn't always the same as a loss.

questions.q: Your account drops 50%. A 50% gain gets you all the way back.
questions.why: False. You need 100%. Halve the account and a 50% gain on what's left only gets you three quarters of the way back. You have to double the half to get to even. The deeper the hole, the harder the climb. That's the whole case for keeping losses small.
questions.lesson_line: Losses are harder to undo than they look. Keep them small.
questions.simple: False. After a 50% drop you need a 100% gain to get back to the peak.

deeper.trap: Many people assume a 50% gain offsets a 50% loss. A given percentage loss always needs a bigger percentage gain to repair, because the gain starts from a smaller base.

questions.q: Your account is down 20% from its high. What gain do you need to get back to that high?
questions.why: 25%. Say the account was $100. Down 20% leaves $80. Getting back to $100 means making $20 on $80, and $20 over $80 is 25%. You climb from a smaller base, so the gain has to be bigger than the loss. Keep the losses small and the climbs stay short.
questions.lesson_line: Down 20% needs up 25%. The deeper the hole, the steeper the climb.
questions.simple: You need 25%, because you climb back from a smaller base than the one you fell from.

deeper.example: The climb back is always steeper than the fall. A 10% loss needs an 11% gain, and a 50% loss needs 100%.

wrong.20%: That assumes the gain equals the loss. You're climbing from a smaller base.
wrong.16.7%: That's the reverse trip, the fall that follows a 20% gain.
wrong.80%: That's the share of the account you still have.

questions.q: Tap the word that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: My account fell from its high of $50,000 to $44,000. That fall from the high is a ___.
questions.why: Drawdown. A drawdown is a fall in account value from a peak to the low after it. It is usually quoted as a percent of the peak. It counts open trades as well as closed losses. A gap is a price move, a loss limit is a rule, and a trailing stop is an order.
questions.lesson_line: Track your drawdown from the account's high, not from where you started.
questions.simple: Drawdown, because the account fell from its high of $50,000 to $44,000.

reasons: fixed before (a computed number removed from the sentence)

questions.q: Tap the term that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: I lost my set amount for the day by 11 a.m., so I hit my ___ and stopped trading.
questions.why: Daily loss limit. Fidelity: some traders set a maximum allowable loss for the day and end their activities when they reach it. Schwab calls it a circuit breaker. A monthly limit counts the whole month, not one day. UCT has no daily loss limit. Our limit is monthly: at 8% down in a calendar month, no new trades for the rest of the month.
questions.lesson_line: A daily loss limit ends your trading for the day. UCT's limit is monthly instead.
questions.simple: Daily loss limit, because you lost the amount you set for the day and then stopped trading.

reasons: the why teaches the owner's rulebook B15 and B16 (no daily limit, a monthly 8% limit)

questions.story: You set yourself a rule: no new trades once you're down $1,000 on the day. By noon you're down $1,050. At 1 p.m. a great setup shows up.
questions.q: Do you take it?
choices: Skip it, but trade after 3 p.m.
Take it to win the loss back
questions.why: Skip it. You're down $1,050 against a $1,000 limit, so you're done for the day. A limit only gets tested when breaking it looks smart, and a great setup is that test. Trading to win it back is revenge trading, and that's how blowups start. We don't use a daily limit ourselves. Ours is monthly: 8% down in a month, no new trades till it ends.
questions.lesson_line: A limit is a wall, not a suggestion.

wrong.Take it to win the loss back: That's revenge trading, the spiral behind a lot of big blowups.
wrong.Raise today's limit to $2,000: A limit you move when it's hit isn't a limit.
The limit ends your whole day, not just one setup.

questions.simple: Skip it and wait for tomorrow. A loss limit only works if you obey it once it's hit.

deeper.trap: The great setup is the trap. Fidelity: once you set a limit, have the discipline to observe it. Schwab calls these limits circuit breakers, and links revenge trading to many blowups.

reasons: the why and deeper teach the owner's rulebook B15 and B16; a daily limit is not a UCT rule

questions.q: You look back over two years of your account. What does its maximum drawdown tell you?
choices: Your largest loss on one trade
The average of all your drawdowns
questions.why: The biggest drop from a peak to a low before a new high. That's the worst stretch your account has lived through. A bounce that doesn't make a new high isn't a new peak, so you keep measuring from the old one. It's about the whole account, not one trade. If you can't stomach that number again, you're sizing too big.
questions.lesson_line: Max drawdown is the worst stretch your account has lived through.

wrong.Your largest loss on one trade: That's one trade. Max drawdown measures the whole account, peak to low.
wrong.The widest stop you've used: That's a stop setting, not a fall in value.
wrong.The average of all your drawdowns: It's the single worst one, not an average.

questions.simple: It's the biggest drop from a peak to a low before the account made a new high.

deeper.example: Investopedia's example: an account peaks at $750,000, falls, bounces to $600,000 and falls again. The drop is still measured from $750,000, because $600,000 was not a new high.

questions.story: Your account climbs from $100,000 to $130,000 and falls to $104,000. It bounces to $120,000, drops to $91,000, then makes a new high.
questions.q: What's your maximum drawdown?
questions.why: 30%. Measure from the $130,000 peak to the lowest point before a new high, $91,000. From $130,000 down to $91,000 is 30%. The bounce to $120,000 never beat $130,000, so it isn't a new peak. That 30% is the hole you lived through, and it's the number to size against.
questions.lesson_line: Max drawdown runs from the highest peak to the lowest low before a new high.

wrong.20%: That's only the first drop. The account fell further before it made a new high.
wrong.24.2%: That starts at the $120,000 bounce. It wasn't a new high, so it isn't the peak.
wrong.9%: That measures from where you started. Drawdown runs from the peak.

questions.simple: Max drawdown is 30%, from the $130,000 high to the $91,000 low before any new high.

deeper.trap: The bounce is the trap. $120,000 looks like a fresh start, but it's below the $130,000 high, so it's not a new peak. Investopedia's own example skips an interim peak of $600,000 for the same reason.

questions.q: A friend says his risk of ruin is high. What is he worried about?
choices: Losses too big to come back from
A gap right past his stop
questions.answer: Losses too big to come back from
questions.why: Losses too big to come back from. Ruin is the account getting so small it can't trade its way back. It doesn't have to mean zero. It's whatever drawdown would make you quit. Big size per trade plus a normal losing run is how you get there. Small risk per trade keeps you in the game.
questions.lesson_line: Survival comes first. An edge is worthless once the account can't trade it.

wrong.The next trade losing: That's one trade. Ruin is about the account surviving a run of them.
wrong.His largest drawdown so far: That's max drawdown, a fall already taken. Risk of ruin is about the odds ahead.
wrong.A gap right past his stop: That's gap risk on one trade. It can cost more than planned, but it's not ruin.

questions.simple: It's the chance your losses get so big the account can't recover.

reasons: stable definition, two publishers (wording differs, key fits both)

deeper.example: Investopedia: the probability of losses big enough to make recovery impossible. Tharp sets ruin at the drawdown where you'd stop trading, a personal level.

questions.q: The smaller the cushion of money behind your losses, the fewer losing trades it takes to wreck the account.
questions.why: True. Ruin is about how many losses your money can soak up before the account can't come back. Thin cushion, and an ordinary losing run finishes it. That's what small risk per trade buys you. Each loss is a small bite out of a big cushion. Same edge, and you're still here to collect it.
questions.lesson_line: Keep the cushion thick. You can't collect an edge with a blown-up account.
questions.simple: True. The less money you have to absorb a losing run, the fewer losses it takes to wreck you.

deeper.example: Investopedia: risk of ruin depends on how many bets are placed and how much capital there is to cushion probable losses. Tharp: a positive-expectancy method makes money over the long term if played at a low enough risk level.

questions.story: Two traders run the same method, which has a positive expectancy. One risks 1% a trade. The other risks 25%.
questions.q: Which one is more likely to blow up the account?
questions.why: The one risking 25%. Same method, same edge, very different size. At 25% a trade, a few losers in a row and most of the account is gone. Every method has losing runs. At 1% a trade the same run is a scratch. We risk under 1% normally, and 2% is the ceiling we never cross.
questions.lesson_line: An edge only pays if you're still around to collect it.

wrong.Neither, edge saves both: An edge is an average. Size decides whether you survive the losing runs on the way.
wrong.The trader risking 1%: Small risk keeps the cushion thick, so a losing run hurts far less.
wrong.Both face the same odds: Same method, different size. At 25% a trade there's almost no cushion.

questions.simple: The one risking 25%. A short losing run at that size leaves too little to recover with.

deeper.trap: The trap is thinking a positive expectancy makes you safe. It's an average over many trades, and it only pays if you survive the losing runs. Tharp sizes a low-risk idea so it survives the worst short-term run.

questions.q: You've got six trades on, each with a stop. What does your portfolio heat add up?
choices: Total open risk across your trades
How fast your best stock rises
questions.answer: Total open risk across your trades
questions.why: Your total open risk. Add up what every trade loses if its stop hits, and that's your heat. It's your worst case if the whole market turns on you at once. We watch it, and it moves with the market. There's no fixed cap. But if you can't name your heat, you don't know what you're risking.
questions.lesson_line: Portfolio heat is what you lose if every stop hits at once.

wrong.How fast your best stock rises: Heat here means risk, not momentum.
wrong.Your single largest position: That's one position's size. Heat adds up the risk on all of them.
wrong.Your account's monthly drawdown: That's a loss already taken. Heat is risk still open.

questions.simple: Heat is what you'd lose if every one of your stops hit at once.

deeper.example: Tharp: the total open risk in your portfolio at any given time. Seykota and Druz call the distributed bet size the heat of the portfolio. Elder's rule keeps the total risk on open positions to 6% of capital.

questions.q: You hold four trades. Each one risks 1.5% of the account to its stop. What's your heat?
questions.why: 6%. Four trades at 1.5% each is 4 times 1.5%, 6% in all. That's what you lose if the market drops hard and every stop hits the same day. Each trade looks small on its own. Together they add up fast, so check the total before you add one more.
questions.lesson_line: Know your total heat before you add one more trade.
questions.simple: Your heat is 6%, because four trades that each risk 1.5% add up to 6%.

wrong.1.5%: That's one trade's risk. You've got three more on.
wrong.5.5%: You added the 4 trades to the 1.5% instead of multiplying.
wrong.4%: That's the number of trades read as a percent.

deeper.example: Seykota and Druz: a portfolio risking 2% on each of five positions has a total heat of 10%.

questions.q: Seven of your eight positions are chip stocks. What kind of risk are you carrying?
choices: Too much money in one area
A stop that fills too late
A gap right past your stop
questions.answer: Too much money in one area
questions.why: Too much money in one area. Seven chip stocks aren't seven bets. Stocks in one group tend to move together, so one bad day for the group hits most of your book at once. That's concentration risk. Being heavy in the leading group is how you catch a big move, and I'm fine with that. Just know your total risk if the whole group turns the same day.
questions.lesson_line: Heavy in one group is fine. Know what you lose if the whole group turns.

wrong.Owning too many positions: That's the opposite problem. Concentration is too much in one place.
wrong.A stop that fills too late: That's how a stop order fills, not where your money sits.
wrong.A gap right past your stop: That's gap risk on one stock. Concentration is about how much sits in one group.

questions.simple: Too much of your money sits in one area, so one bad day for that group hits most of your book.

deeper.example: FINRA: the risk of amplified losses from having a large portion of your holdings in one investment, asset class or market segment. Same-industry holdings tend to be highly correlated.

questions.story: You hold five chip stocks. Each one risks 1% of the account to its stop.
questions.q: Semis get hit hard tomorrow. How much of the account is at risk?
choices: About 5%, if all five stops hit
All the money in the stocks
questions.answer: About 5%, if all five stops hit
questions.why: About 5%, if all five stops hit. Chip stocks tend to move together, so what hits one is likely to hit the others. Your risk isn't 1%. It's 1% five times, 5% in all. Know that number before the bad day comes, not after.
questions.lesson_line: Stocks in one group tend to fall together, so their stops can hit together.

wrong.About 1%, one stop will hit: Stocks in one group move together. When one falls hard, the others likely fall too.
wrong.All the money in the stocks: That's what you put in. Each stop is set to cost 1%.
wrong.About 0.2%, 1% split five ways: Each stock risks its own 1%. The risks add up, they don't split.

questions.simple: About 5%. Chip stocks tend to fall together, so all five stops can hit at once.

deeper.trap: Five tickers can feel like five separate bets. FINRA's point is correlation: same-industry stocks tend to move together. A bad day for chips can trigger every stop at once.

find.label: Account at risk, all stops hit

questions.q: You own three chip stocks and a chip ETF. That spreads out your risk.
questions.why: False. A chip ETF is full of chip stocks, likely the same ones you already own. So you added more of the same bet. Stocks in one group tend to move together. Different tickers, same risk. Look at what a fund holds before you call your book spread out.
questions.lesson_line: Look under the hood. Different tickers can carry the same risk.
questions.simple: False. A chip ETF holds more chip stocks, so you own more of the same bet.

deeper.trap: The hidden overlap is the trap. FINRA's own example is tech stocks, plus a tech fund, plus the tech stocks inside an index fund you own, all one concentration.

questions.q: You hold three winners, all well above where you bought. What does your open risk measure?
choices: Price now to stop, all positions
Entry to stop on your newest trade
Money spent on your open positions
Profit you have not yet sold
questions.answer: Price now to stop, all positions
questions.why: Price now down to the stop, across every position. Not from your entry, from today's price. As a winner runs, the gap between price and stop grows, and so does what you could give back. Raise the stop and open risk shrinks. That's why open risk can climb in a great week.
questions.lesson_line: As a winner runs, open risk grows unless your stop follows it.

wrong.Entry to stop on your newest trade: That's the first risk, R, on one trade.
wrong.Money spent on your open positions: That's what you put in, not what you can lose.
wrong.Profit you have not yet sold: That's open profit, measured from your entry. Open risk runs from today's price down to the stop.

questions.simple: It's what all your positions lose if they fall from today's price down to their stops.

reasons: stable definition named for Tharp, Elder agrees

deeper.example: Tharp: the difference between the current price and the stop for all positions you have open. He calls it another word for portfolio heat.

questions.q: You own 100 shares bought at $50. They trade at $62 now, and you've raised your stop to $55. What's your open risk?
questions.why: $700. Open risk runs from today's $62 down to your $55 stop. That's $7 a share, times 100 shares, $700. Your stop sits over your $50 buy, so the trade can't lose money anymore, short of a gap. But $700 of open profit can still go back. Keep raising the stop as it works and that number shrinks.
questions.lesson_line: Open profit above your stop is still at risk.
questions.simple: Your open risk is $700, because 100 shares can fall from $62 to your $55 stop.

deeper.example: Here the stop at $55 keeps part of the gain. Every dollar the stock sits above $55 is still exposed. Raising the stop shrinks open risk.

wrong.$1,200: That's your open gain from your entry, not the risk down to the stop.
wrong.$500: That's the profit locked in above your entry, not the open risk.
wrong.$7: That's the risk on one share. You hold 100.

questions.q: Your breakout is up 3R and you decide to move to a breakeven stop. Where does the stop go?
choices: Up to the price you paid
questions.answer: Up to the price you paid
questions.why: Up to the price you paid. From here the trade can't turn into a loser, short of a gap. We make that move somewhere between 2R and 5R, or when we take the first sell. It's a judgment, not a fixed spot. Do it too early and a normal dip knocks you out of a good trade.
questions.lesson_line: A breakeven stop keeps a winner from turning into a loser.

wrong.Just under today's high: That's a very tight trail. A breakeven stop sits at your entry.
wrong.Just under the day's low: That's where your first stop went. A breakeven stop uses your entry price.
wrong.Halfway to your entry: That cuts the risk but the trade can still lose. Breakeven is your entry.

questions.simple: It goes up to the price you paid, so the trade can't turn into a loss.

deeper.example: TradeStation places it at the average entry price of the position. O'Neil's version: don't let a stock fall back below your purchase price.

questions.q: With your stop at breakeven, a gap below your entry still fills you at your entry.
questions.why: False. A breakeven stop is a stop market order. When price falls back to entry, a market order is sent. After a gap down, the fill can be well below your entry. The stop price is a trigger, not a guaranteed price. TradeStation also notes its math ignores commission and slippage.
questions.lesson_line: Breakeven is a plan to exit at entry, not a promise of no loss.
questions.simple: False: at your entry the stop turns into a market order, and after a gap it can fill well below.

deeper.trap: Breakeven feels like a free trade. It is not. Schwab: after a gap down, the fill can be significantly lower than the stop price. A stop at your entry can still end in a loss.

reasons: Tier 1 fact plus two publishers agree

questions.story: Your breakout is up 1R, so you move the stop to your entry. The stock dips a few cents under your entry, sells you out, then rallies hard.
questions.q: What did that early breakeven stop cost you?
choices: It let normal swings stop you out
It locked in a gain on the trade
It capped your upside at your entry
It made the stop a limit order
questions.answer: It let normal swings stop you out
questions.why: It let a normal dip stop you out. At 1R your entry sits right in the noise, and a stop that close gets hit by regular day-to-day swings. We wait until somewhere between 2R and 5R, or the first sell, before moving to breakeven. That gives the stock room to work. Getting shaken out of a winner costs more than a small loss.
questions.lesson_line: Move to breakeven too early and the noise takes you out of good trades.

wrong.It made the stop a limit order: A breakeven stop is still a stop that sells at market.
wrong.It locked in a gain on the trade: A breakeven stop sits at your entry. Filled there, it saves you a loss but keeps no gain.
wrong.It capped your upside at your entry: A stop limits the downside. Your upside was open until the stop sold you out.

questions.simple: Moving to breakeven at 1R let an ordinary dip stop you out before the real move.

deeper.trap: A breakeven stop trades one risk for another. It shrinks the loss if the trade fails, but ordinary dips can now take you out. Schwab warns a stop too close can be triggered by regular daily swings. Dave Mabe never moves to breakeven at all.

questions.q: You want a stop that climbs as the stock climbs but never moves down. Which one is that?
questions.why: A trailing stop. It follows the price up, and when the stock falls it stays put. That lets you keep most of a big move without guessing the top. Ours trails the 9 EMA for fast movers, or the 20 EMA for steadier ones. Sell what's left on a close below it.
questions.lesson_line: A trailing stop moves one way: with your profit.

wrong.Breakeven stop: That sits at your entry price and stays there.
wrong.Initial stop: That's the first stop, the one that sets R.
wrong.Stop-limit order: That's about the fill price once triggered, not about following the trend.

questions.simple: A trailing stop. It follows the price up and stays put when the price falls.

deeper.example: Schwab: the stop price can move higher indefinitely, but it can never move lower.

questions.q: You set a 20% trailing stop. The stock peaks at $85, then starts to slide. Where's your stop now?
questions.why: $68. The stop trails 20% under the high. 20% of $85 is $17, and $85 minus $17 is $68. It stays there as the stock slides. A percent trail measures from the highest price, never from your entry. Ours isn't a percent, though. We trail the 9 or 20 EMA and sell on a close below it.
questions.lesson_line: A trailing stop measures from the high, not from your entry.
questions.simple: Your stop is $68, 20% under the $85 high, and it never moves down.

deeper.counter: Tharp's example: a 25% trail under a $60 high sits at $45 and is never moved back down.

wrong.$102: You added 20% to the high instead of taking it off.
wrong.$85: That's the high itself. The trail sits 20% under it.
wrong.$106: You divided the high instead of taking 20% off it.

questions.story: You bought at $30. The stock ran to $60, and your 25% trailing stop now sits at $45. Then the stock turns down.
questions.q: If the stop fills at $45, what do you keep?
questions.why: $15 a share, half the gain. You paid $30 and sell at $45, so you keep $15. At the $60 high you were up $30, so the trail gave half of it back. That's the price of staying in for a big run. The trail is 25% of the price, not 25% of the gain.
questions.lesson_line: A trailing stop gives some back so you can stay for the rest.

wrong.$30 a share, the whole gain: The stop sits 25% under the high, so part of the gain goes back.
wrong.$45 a share, the stop price: $45 is the price you sell at, not your profit. You paid $30.
wrong.$22.50 a share, 75% of the gain: That takes 25% off the $30 gain. The trail is 25% off the $60 price.

questions.simple: You keep $15 a share, half the gain, because you sell at $45 after paying $30.

deeper.trap: The trail only moves one way. Tharp's own example: if the stock falls from $60 to $50, the exit stays at $45. Lowering it to give the trade room hands back the profit the trail was built to keep.

questions.q: Set your trail wider and you give back more profit when the trend finally turns.
questions.why: True. A wide trail lets a real reversal eat more of your gain before you're out. Too tight has its own cost: a normal dip shakes you out before the trend is done. So it's a trade-off. We trail the 9 EMA for fast movers and the 20 EMA for steadier ones. Match the line to how the stock trends.
questions.lesson_line: Too wide gives back profit. Too tight gets shaken out. Match the trail to the stock.
questions.simple: True. A trail set far away lets price fall further before you're out, so you give back more.

deeper.counter: A wider trail isn't always worse. A tight trail can stop you out on a normal dip and miss the rest of the run. The wide trail loses more only at the final turn. Investopedia warns about both sides.

questions.q: Tap the word that fits our rule.
questions.sentence: Hold your winners by selling partials into strength and ___ the rising moving averages.
questions.why: Trailing. In the owner's words: hold your winners by selling partials into strength and trailing the rising moving averages.
questions.lesson_line: Sell some into strength. Trail the rest under the rising averages.

questions.q: You pull up a daily chart and see an ATR of $1.18. What's that telling you?
choices: How much it moves in a normal day
How far price is from its average
questions.answer: How much it moves in a normal day
questions.why: How much it moves in a normal day. ATR averages each day's true range, over 14 days on most charts. An ATR of $1.18 means the stock moves about $1.18 a day. It tells you size, not direction. I use it to keep a stop outside the normal noise.
questions.lesson_line: ATR tells you how far a stock normally moves in a day.

wrong.Your average loss per trade: That comes from your trade log, not the chart.
wrong.How far price is from its average: That's a stretch read. ATR averages the size of each day's range.
wrong.Its average volume over 14 days: That's a volume average. ATR uses price ranges.

questions.simple: It shows how much the stock moves in a normal day, about $1.18 here.

deeper.example: J. Welles Wilder built the Average True Range to measure volatility. Investopedia: if the ATR is $1.18, the price has an average range of movement of $1.18 per trading day.

questions.q: ATR has been rising all week. That means the stock is heading higher.
questions.why: False. ATR measures how big the moves are, not which way. A stock falling hard shows a rising ATR, same as one ripping up. So a rising ATR never gives you a buy. Read direction from price and the averages. Read ATR for how much room a stop needs.
questions.lesson_line: ATR says how big the moves are, never which way.
questions.simple: False. ATR only shows how big the moves are, and it rises in a sharp fall too.

questions.story: One stock trades at $300 with a daily ATR of $6. Another trades at $20 with a daily ATR of $1.50.
questions.q: Which one moves more for its price?
choices: The $300 one, its ATR is bigger
questions.why: The $20 one, about 7.5% a day. ATR is in dollars, so a pricey stock always shows the bigger number. Put it in percent: $1.50 over $20 is 7.5%. $6 over $300 is a lot less. I always read ATR as a percent of price. That's what tells you how much room a stop needs.
questions.lesson_line: Compare ATR as a percent of price. Dollars alone mislead.

wrong.About the same: For its price, the $20 stock moves several times as much.
wrong.The $300 one, its ATR is bigger: A $6 ATR on a $300 stock is a small move for its price.
wrong.The $20 one, 1.5% a day: That reads the $1.50 ATR as a percent. On a $20 stock it's 7.5%.

questions.simple: The $20 stock. Its $1.50 range is 7.5% of its price, far more than $6 is of $300.

deeper.trap: A bigger ATR number isn't a bigger move. StockCharts: ATR isn't shown as a percent of the close, so low-priced stocks show lower ATR values and the raw numbers aren't comparable.

questions.q: You're buying a stock resting on its 20 EMA and 50 SMA. You want your stop under the lines. Where exactly?
choices: A little under the lower line
Right on the line, no cushion
questions.answer: A little under the lower line
questions.why: A little under the lower line. When price rests on the 20 EMA and 50 SMA, those lines are the support. If it closes through both, the idea's broken. So the stop goes under the lower one, with a small cushion for wicks. How big a cushion is a read of the chart: how much this stock pokes through its lines. Our first choice is still a few cents under the low of the day.
questions.lesson_line: Under the lower line, with room for a wick. Or a few cents under the low of the day.

wrong.Right on the line, no cushion: Price often pokes through a line and comes right back. No cushion, and a wick takes you out.
wrong.A flat 10% under your entry: That ignores the chart, and 10% is twice the most we'll take on a stop.
wrong.Three ATRs under the high: That's the Chandelier Exit, a trailing stop for a winner, not where a new stop goes.

questions.simple: A little under the lower of the two lines, with a small cushion for wicks.

reasons: house setup plan not yet reviewed against the rulebook

questions.story: Yesterday the stock closed at $50. Today it gaps up: high $54, low $52.50.
questions.q: What's today's true range?
questions.why: $4.00. True range is the biggest of three distances: high to low, high to yesterday's close, and low to yesterday's close. High to the $50 close is $4.00, and that's the biggest of the three. After a gap up, high to yesterday's close wins. That's how the gap gets counted in the stock's range.
questions.lesson_line: True range is the biggest of three distances. Check all three.

wrong.$5.50: You added the high-to-low and high-to-close distances. True range takes the biggest one.
wrong.$6.50: You added the two distances from yesterday's close.
wrong.$8.00: You added all three. True range is the biggest one, not a sum.

questions.simple: True range is $4.00, because after the gap up the high is farthest from yesterday's $50 close.

questions.q: A trailing stop hangs a set number of ATRs under the highest high since you bought. What's it called?
questions.why: The Chandelier Exit. It hangs under the highest high like a chandelier from the ceiling. As the high climbs, the stop climbs with it. A jumpier stock has a bigger ATR, so its stop hangs further down. It's a fine tool, but ours is simpler: we trail the 9 or 20 EMA.
questions.lesson_line: The Chandelier Exit lets the stock's swing set the trail.

wrong.Breakeven stop: That sits at your entry price.
wrong.Initial stop: That's your first stop, set when you buy.
wrong.Moving-average trail: That trails a moving average. The Chandelier Exit uses the high minus ATRs.

questions.simple: The Chandelier Exit. It hangs a trailing stop a few ATRs under the highest high.

deeper.example: Chuck LeBeau developed it. StockCharts' standard version hangs three ATR values below the 22-period high.

questions.q: The 22-day high is $80 and the 22-day ATR is $2.50. Where does a 3-ATR Chandelier Exit sit?
questions.why: $72.50. Three ATRs is 3 times $2.50, $7.50. $80 minus $7.50 is $72.50. As new highs print, the exit climbs with them. A wilder stock has a bigger ATR, so its exit hangs further down.
questions.lesson_line: Chandelier Exit: the 22-day high minus three ATRs.
questions.simple: The exit sits at $72.50, three ATRs of $2.50 under the $80 high.

wrong.$7.50: That's the three ATRs. You still take them off the high.
wrong.$70.00: You went down four ATRs instead of three.
wrong.$25.00: You used 22 ATRs, the lookback, instead of three.

deeper.example: StockCharts' formula: Chandelier Exit (long) = 22-day High - ATR(22) x 3.

questions.story: You trail jumpy tech stocks with a 3-ATR Chandelier Exit. Normal pullbacks keep stopping you out before the trend resumes.
questions.q: What do you change on your next trade?
questions.why: A higher multiplier. Jumpy tech names swing more, so the trail needs more room or normal pullbacks take you out. Set it before you buy, never by widening a stop you already hold. Our stop only moves up. A wider trail costs more per share if it hits, so buy fewer shares and keep the dollars at risk the same.
questions.lesson_line: Give a jumpy stock more room, and buy fewer shares to pay for it.

wrong.A flat 2% stop instead: A flat percent ignores how much this stock swings.
wrong.A smaller ATR multiplier: That tightens the trail. You'd get shaken out even more.
wrong.Same stop, half the shares: Fewer shares cut the dollars lost, but the same trail still shakes you out.

questions.simple: Use a higher ATR multiplier next time and buy fewer shares, so a jumpy stock gets room.

deeper.trap: The trap is widening the stop on a trade you already hold. The stop only moves up, never down or wider. StockCharts: volatile stocks may need a higher multiplier to reduce whipsaws, and it names techs.

questions.q: You're sizing two trades: a calm stock and one that swings twice as much. What does volatility-based sizing do?
choices: Same share count on every trade
Size set by your win rate
questions.why: Smaller size in the jumpier stock. The more a stock swings, the fewer shares you hold, so each position moves the account about the same. It's the same idea as sizing from the stop: a wider stop for a wilder stock means fewer shares. Never more shares just because a stock moves a lot.
questions.lesson_line: Let the stock's swing set the size, so each position moves the account about the same.

wrong.Bigger size for jumpier stocks: Backwards. Bigger swings call for fewer shares.
wrong.Same share count on every trade: That ignores both the stop and the swing.
wrong.Size set by your win rate: Win rate doesn't measure how much a stock moves.

questions.simple: It gives the jumpier stock a smaller size, so each position moves the account about the same.

deeper.example: Tharp's percent volatility model caps the volatility in each position, measured by the average true range, at a set percent of equity. Investopedia: higher volatility may require smaller positions.

questions.q: You can set a trailing stop a fixed percent or a fixed dollar amount under the price.
questions.why: True. Your broker lets you set the trail either way, a percent or a dollar amount. As the price climbs, the stop follows by that amount. When the price drops, the stop stays fixed. Ours trails a moving average instead, the 9 or 20 EMA, and sells on a close below it.
questions.lesson_line: A broker's trail sits a set percent or dollar amount from the price.
questions.simple: True. A trailing stop can sit a set percent or a set dollar amount under the price.

reasons: one source only (SEC Investor.gov bulletin), which refused WebFetch (403) on 2026-11-12, so it was not re-read this run

deeper.example: The SEC: a trailing stop price is a defined percentage or dollar amount above or below the current market price.

questions.q: After a 10% loss, you need an 11% gain to get back to even.
questions.why: True. Every loss needs a bigger gain to repair it. Down 10% needs 11%, and down 50% needs 100%.
questions.lesson_line: Losses are repaired by bigger gains. Down 10% needs 11%.

questions.q: A high win rate on its own doesn't prove your method makes money.
questions.why: True. Win rate counts how often you win, not how much. Win most of the time, take a few big losses, and you can still be down. Some setups that hit often bleed money this way. Check your average win and loss in R next to it. Expectancy is the number that tells you.
questions.lesson_line: Win rate alone proves nothing. The size of the losses matters too.
questions.simple: True. If the losing trades are much bigger than the winners, a high win rate can still lose money.

deeper.example: Investopedia: if the losing trades have dollar losses three times as large as the winning trades' gains, the trader has a losing strategy. Tharp notes some high hit-rate systems lose money through occasional large losses.

questions.q: You don't move your stop to breakeven the day you buy. It waits until the trade has built up some profit.
questions.why: True. Breakeven comes after the trade has paid you something. We make the move somewhere from 2R to 5R, or at the first sell. Put it at your entry on day one and there's no room at all. The first normal dip back to your price takes you out. Some platforms automate it: the stop only goes in once the profit passes a floor you set.
questions.lesson_line: Let the trade pay you first. Then the stop goes to breakeven.
questions.simple: True. You move the stop up to breakeven only after the trade shows a profit, never right after you buy.

deeper.counter: TradeStation's breakeven stop works this way: it does nothing until the profit passes a floor you set, then places a stop at your average entry price. Not every trader uses one. Dave Mabe never moves a stop to breakeven. O'Neil says not to let a worthwhile profit fall back below your purchase price.

questions.q: True range counts an overnight gap that a plain high-to-low range would miss.
questions.why: True. Say a stock gaps up and holds tight all day. Its high-to-low range looks quiet, but the real move happened overnight. True range also measures from yesterday's close, so the gap counts. That's why ATR is built on true range, not just the day's range.
questions.lesson_line: True range counts the gap from yesterday's close.
questions.simple: True. True range measures from the prior close too, so a gap counts in the stock's range.

deeper.example: StockCharts: a volatility formula based only on the high-low range would fail to capture volatility from gap or limit moves. Wilder built the Average True Range to capture it.

questions.q: Normal day, normal setup, nothing special about it. How much of the account do you put at risk?
choices: Up to 5% on the best ones
questions.why: Under 1% of the account. That's normal for us. Even our best setups top out at 1.5%, and 2% is the ceiling we never cross. Small risk per trade is what lets you sit through a losing run and still be here for the big winners. Size up on quality, not on feeling.

wrong.2% of the account, every time: 2% is our absolute ceiling, not our normal.
wrong.1.5% of the account, every time: 1.5% is the most any grade gets. It's a top, not the normal.
wrong.Up to 5% on the best ones: Our ceiling is 2% a trade. Even the best grade gets 1.5% at most.

questions.simple: Under 1% of the account. That's our normal, and 2% is the most we ever risk.
questions.lesson_line: Our normal risk is under 1% a trade. 2% is the ceiling.

questions.q: It's mid-month and your account is down 8% since the month began. What now?
choices: No new trades until next month
Sit out the rest of the week
Keep going, your stops cover it
questions.answer: No new trades until next month
questions.why: No new trades until next month. 8% down in a calendar month is our brake. You stop opening trades for the rest of the month. We don't use a daily or a weekly limit, just this one. It stops a bad month from turning into a disaster, right when you're most tempted to press. Use the time to review what went wrong.
questions.lesson_line: Down 8% in a month, we stop opening trades until the next one.

wrong.Stop for today, back tomorrow: We don't use a daily limit. The brake is monthly, so the rest of the month is off.
wrong.Sit out the rest of the week: We don't use a weekly limit either. At 8% down it's the rest of the month.
wrong.Keep going, your stops cover it: A stop limits one trade. The monthly limit protects the whole account.

questions.simple: No new trades until next month. At 8% down in a month, we stop opening trades.

conflicts: Risk/reward naming. Investopedia (riskrewardratio.asp) writes the ratio risk first, as potential loss / potential gain, so 'a 1:2 risk/reward ratio' means risk $1 to make $2 and lower is better. Van Tharp's glossary entry 'Reward-to-Risk Ratio' means yearly return / maximum drawdown, or average win / average loss. Schwab's 5 Elements page says 'risk-to-reward ratio ... how many dollars do you expect to gain for each dollar you commit to the position', which mixes it up with return on capital. The file keys only what the ratio compares (entry to stop vs entry to target, q19) and the dollars made per dollar risked (q20), and names 1:3 as Investopedia's way of writing it.

Win/loss ratio. Investopedia defines it as winning trades / losing trades; Schwab's 5 Elements page calls 'the percentage of your trades that have been profitable' a win/loss ratio. Investopedia's own example also says a 12/18 = 0.67 ratio 'means that you are losing 67% of the time' while giving the win rate as 40% (the loss rate is 60%). Not keyed: the file teaches 'win rate' (Tharp and Investopedia agree: winning trades out of all closed trades) and never asks win/loss ratio.

Open risk vs heat base. Tharp's glossary measures open risk from the CURRENT price to the stop and calls it 'another word for portfolio heat'; Seykota and Druz describe heat as the bet size risked per instrument; F9.06 notes R is measured from the entry. The file measures open risk from the current price (q48, q49), keys heat only as the total of what every stop would lose (q43, q44, q46), and never keys which base heat uses.

Heat caps. Tharp's glossary says portfolio heat 'generally should not exceed 20%'; Elder's rule (Incredible Charts) caps open risk at 6%; docs/study/sizing_rule.md section 5 says 10% but marks it 'App cap', not an owner answer. No cap is keyed anywhere in this file.

Investopedia, Trailing Stops (Henry Hoenig): its NVDA example writes '$99 (110 - (11 x 0.10))' (the arithmetic is 110 - 110 x 0.10), and it says swing trading 'by definition is not about riding a trend'. Neither is cited; only its definitional lines on stops set too close or too far, and on moving-average trails, are used.

Investopedia, How Stop-Loss Orders Help Limit Investment Losses and Risk: its earnings example says the stop 'triggers at $90, limiting the loss' after a gap down, contradicting its own gap paragraph, the SEC and FINRA. Only the gap paragraph (f102) is cited.

Investopedia, Understanding the 2% Rule (James Chen): its AAPL example writes '$50,000 x 0.02%' (2% is meant) and '4% loss ($1,000 / $30)' (67 shares x $30 is about $2,010, which is about 4% of $50,000), and its 'Practical Example' treats 2% as an allocation cap, contradicting its own definition (risk per trade). Only the definition (f99), the gap/slippage line (f100) and the volatility-sizing line (f101) are cited; q26 builds its own gap example with a calc.

True range. Van Tharp's ATR glossary lists the third true-range term as 'today's low minus yesterday's close' without the absolute value; Investopedia and StockCharts use absolute values. True range (q62) is keyed on Investopedia and StockCharts only; Tharp's ATR entry is not cited.

ATR smoothing. Investopedia's key takeaway says ATR is 'typically derived from the 14-day simple moving average' of true range; StockCharts uses Wilder's smoothing ([prior ATR x 13 + current TR] / 14). The file says only that ATR averages the true range, usually over 14 days.

Breakeven stops. TradeStation defines the breakeven stop (a stop at the average entry price once a set profit is reached); O'Neil (AAII) says not to let a worthwhile profit fall back below the purchase price; Dave Mabe (IBKR Campus) never moves a stop to breakeven. The file keys the definition (q50) and both costs, gaps (q51) and shakeouts (q52), and never says when to move to breakeven or that you always should.

Risk of ruin. Investopedia defines it as the probability of losses too big to recover from; Tharp's glossary defines 'ruin' as the drawdown at which you would stop trading (a personal level, not necessarily zero). q40's key ('odds of losing too much to recover') fits both, and the why gives both.

Seykota and Druz (s23): the line 'If you risk too much, you eventually run to ruin' is the magazine's introduction to the article on its product page, not necessarily the authors' words; the file credits it to the magazine's page in the claim and never quotes it as Seykota's.

R-multiple by name. Only Van Tharp defines 'R-multiple' among the sources found: the Van Tharp Institute pages and his own January 2007 article in Stocks & Commodities (an independent publisher, Technical Analysis, Inc.). No Investopedia, Schwab, Fidelity, StockCharts or IBKR page defining the term was found. The definitional R and R-multiple questions also cite Investopedia's matching 'trade risk is the dollar difference between the entry price and the stop-loss'. Checker to judge whether Tharp in two publications meets the two-publisher rule; the computed R-multiple items (q07, q09) carry calcs.
Chandelier Exit creator: Investopedia spells him 'Chuck LeBeau', StockCharts 'Charles Le Beau'; the same person. The file uses 'Chuck LeBeau'.
